title: Epicurus on Death — can a loss harm someone who never experiences it?
when: Epicurus (341–270 BCE) developed this ethics in the late fourth and early third centuries BCE, founding his Garden school in Athens around 306 BCE. The exact date of the Letter to Menoeceus is unknown; it survives in Diogenes Laertius’s much later compilation.
people: Epicurus; Lucretius, a later Epicurean; modern philosophers debating posthumous harm.
origin: Ancient Greek philosophy, especially Epicurus’s Athenian Garden community.
idea: Epicurus argues death is “nothing to us” because good and bad depend on awareness, while death is the absence of sensation. While alive, we are not dead; once dead, no subject remains to experience being dead. So anticipating nonexistence need not poison life, and happiness need not depend on living forever. This is part of a broader ethical therapy: Epicurus thought understanding nature and the soul could loosen fear of divine punishment after death. The argument does not show that dying cannot hurt, or settle whether death harms us by depriving us of future goods; philosophers still dispute that premise.
relevance: Epicurus redirects attention from an imagined afterlife to present life, friendship, and modest desires. The argument remains a sharp test of what counts as harm: must a loss be experienced, or can missing future goods matter without awareness? It helps frame debates about mortality and end-of-life ethics, while not implying that bereavement is trivial.
